report:
### Conclusion
The claim is **true**. Extensive observational studies and clinical registries consistently show that bystander hands-only (compression-only) CPR is associated with significantly higher survival rates after adult out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) compared to receiving no bystander CPR.

### Evidence
- **Survival Improvement:** Registry data indicate that immediate bystander CPR doubles or triples the chance of survival following OHCA (https://cpr.heart.org/en/resources/cpr-facts-and-stats/). Clinical cohort studies confirm that both hands-only CPR and conventional CPR substantially increase survival compared to no bystander intervention (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9207566/).
- **Efficacy and Community Impact:** According to the American Heart Association, hands-only CPR offers adult sudden cardiac arrest victims a similar chance of survival as traditional CPR with rescue breaths (https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/circulationaha.107.189380). Public endorsement of compression-only CPR has raised bystander intervention rates, leading to improved survival to hospital discharge (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/186668).
- **Important Context:** Hands-only CPR is intended primarily for adult sudden cardiac arrest. Standard CPR involving rescue breaths remains preferable for non-cardiac etiologies, such as pediatric cardiac arrest, drowning, or severe respiratory depression.

Overall, performing bystander hands-only CPR provides a clear and substantial survival benefit over providing no CPR.
